items.title: Restoring an Encrypted SAP HANA Backup to Another System
items.author: neilaspin
items.text:
This document references: https://help.sap.com/docs/SAP_HANA_PLATFORM/6b94445c94ae495c83a19646e7c3fd56/7def3297f93842a6b04f4d3f77ae07f6.html?locale=en-US 
 A tenant backup taken on PRD with backup encryption on, restored into the QAS tenant after importing PRD's root keys. 
 Setup 
 Two EC2 hosts in one VPC (us-east-2), built with Terraform: r5.xlarge, SLES for SAP, gp3 volumes for /hana/data, /hana/log and /hana/shared. HANA 2.00.083 (SPS08) installed on each with hdblcm from an Ansible playbook, one SID per host. 
 locals {
 # One entry per HANA system. Key = SID.
 systems = {
 PRD = { cidr = "10.1.1.0/24" }
 QAS = { cidr = "10.1.2.0/24" }
 }
}

resource "aws_instance" "hana" {
 for_each = local.systems
 ami = local.sles_sap_ami
 instance_type = "r5.xlarge"
 subnet_id = aws_subnet.hana[each.key].id
 tags = { Name = "hana-${lower(each.key)}", SID = each.key }
} 
 The SID comes from the Ansible inventory, one per host: 
 [hana]
prd ansible_host=<prd-public-ip> hana_sid=PRD
qas ansible_host=<qas-public-ip> hana_sid=QAS 
 Each install has SYSTEMDB plus a tenant named after the SID. 
 Encryption state on PRD 
 As prdadm: 
 hdbsql -i 00 -d SYSTEMDB -u SYSTEM -p '<password>' \
 "SELECT DATABASE_NAME, SCOPE, IS_ENCRYPTION_ACTIVE FROM SYS_DATABASES.M_ENCRYPTION_OVERVIEW ORDER BY 1,2" 
 DATABASE_NAME,SCOPE,IS_ENCRYPTION_ACTIVE
"PRD","BACKUP","TRUE"
"PRD","LOG","TRUE"
"PRD","PERSISTENCE","TRUE"
"SYSTEMDB","BACKUP","TRUE"
"SYSTEMDB","LOG","TRUE"
"SYSTEMDB","PERSISTENCE","TRUE" 
 All three scopes were already on after the install. Nothing was set for encryption in the hdblcm response file. 
 Root key backup on PRD 
 The tenant controls its own key management, so the root key commands run in the tenant, not SYSTEMDB. 
 # Password that protects the root key backup file. Needed again on QAS.
hdbsql -i 00 -d PRD -u SYSTEM -p '<password>' \
 "ALTER SYSTEM SET ENCRYPTION ROOT KEYS BACKUP PASSWORD \"<rootkey-password>\""

# Export the tenant's root keys
hdbsql -i 00 -d PRD -u SYSTEM -p '<password>' \
 "BACKUP ENCRYPTION ROOT KEYS USING FILE ('/hana/backup/PRD_rootkeys.rkb')" 
 HANA appends _rootkeys to the path given, so the file is /hana/backup/PRD_rootkeys.rkb_rootkeys. 
 Data backup of the PRD tenant 
 From SYSTEMDB: 
 hdbsql -i 00 -d SYSTEMDB -u SYSTEM -p '<password>' \
 "BACKUP DATA FOR PRD USING FILE ('/hana/backup/PRD_full')" 
 -rw-r----- 1 prdadm sapsys 159744 Nov 14 09:10 /hana/backup/PRD_full_databackup_0_1
-rw-r----- 1 prdadm sapsys 83898368 Nov 14 09:10 /hana/backup/PRD_full_databackup_2_1
-rw-r----- 1 prdadm sapsys 2885693440 Nov 14 09:11 /hana/backup/PRD_full_databackup_3_1 
 Copy to QAS 
 I copied the backup files and the root key file to QAS's /hana/backup over the private network, then gave them to qasadm: 
 # On PRD as ec2-user, connected with ssh -A
sudo --preserve-env=SSH_AUTH_SOCK scp \
 /hana/backup/PRD_full_databackup_* /hana/backup/PRD_rootkeys.rkb_rootkeys \
 ec2-user@<qas-private-ip>:/tmp/

# On QAS
sudo mv /tmp/PRD_* /hana/backup/
sudo chown qasadm:sapsys /hana/backup/PRD_* 
 Recovery without the root keys 
 Before importing anything, stop the QAS tenant and try the recovery as it is: 
 hdbsql -i 00 -d SYSTEMDB -u SYSTEM -p '<password>' "ALTER SYSTEM STOP DATABASE QAS"
hdbsql -i 00 -d SYSTEMDB -u SYSTEM -p '<password>' "RECOVER DATA FOR QAS USING FILE ('/hana/backup/PRD_full') CLEAR LOG" 
 * 448: recovery could not be completed: [110126] Backup rootkey d7b546e7cd850c2d4b05a77ac7fe569b9e06ad6aece831ee6b01e080a73ff428 is required for decryption of backup files, but not found in key store. Please make sure you have provided the necessary keys before recovery., [301103] No root key matching hash=d7b546e7cd850c2d4b05a77ac7fe569b9e06ad6aece831ee6b01e080a73ff428 SQLSTATE: HY000 
 The error names the hash of the backup root key it needs. QAS can't read the backup until PRD's root keys are imported. (This output is from a separate run on rebuilt systems, so the hash differs from the key hashes below.) 
 Import PRD's root keys into QAS 
 The tenant is still stopped. 
 hdbnsutil -recoverRootKeys takes a database ID, not a name. The second number in the data volume directory is the tenant's ID: 
 ls /hana/data/QAS/mnt00001/ 
 hdb00001
hdb00002.00003
hdb00003.00003
nameserver.lck 
 QAS's tenant is dbid 3. Check the file and password before importing: 
 hdbnsutil -validateRootKeysBackup /hana/backup/PRD_rootkeys.rkb_rootkeys --password=<rootkey-password> --printMetaData 
 Backup Version: 1
Backup Creation Date: 2026-11-14 9:9:33
Printing Root Key Metadata for dbid: 3
| Key Purpose | Key Version | Key State | Key Hash |
| BACKUP | 0 | Active | 329926ac1a6f647bbbfaad8c251e28baea1f495e2f83847fb4946bb679de1d4a |
| DPAPI | 0 | Active | 07238d4a9bb865ee513945baa354d5c0064e34d8c16e19befac68886ac3b8809 |
| LOG | 0 | Active | b21c77bd2416035e8372fd1885b2a06846feec43ed5fb2bfe1ac73fbdcde2bcf |
| PERSISTENCE | 0 | Active | d2c80e38fcd7e5ef3a2c04bdadbb1ad1f5918917f9d04aa8d77f431ed2521849 |
Total number of Root Keys in backup file: 4
Successfully validated SSFS backup file /hana/backup/PRD_rootkeys.rkb_rootkeys
done. 
 Import, as qasadm. This replaces the QAS tenant's own root keys: 
 hdbnsutil -recoverRootKeys /hana/backup/PRD_rootkeys.rkb_rootkeys --dbid=3 --password=<rootkey-password> --type=ALL 
 Recover 
 hdbsql -i 00 -d SYSTEMDB -u SYSTEM -p '<password>' \
 "RECOVER DATA FOR QAS USING FILE ('/hana/backup/PRD_full') CLEAR LOG" 
 Check 
 hdbsql -i 00 -d SYSTEMDB -u SYSTEM -p '<password>' -A "SELECT DATABASE_NAME, ACTIVE_STATUS FROM M_DATABASES" 
 | DATABASE | ACT |
| -------- | --- |
| SYSTEMDB | YES |
| QAS | YES | 
 The backup catalog on QAS now starts with PRD's backup: 
 hdbsql -i 00 -d QAS -u SYSTEM -p '<password>' -A -j \
 "SELECT TOP 3 SYS_START_TIME, BACKUP_ID, ENTRY_TYPE_NAME, STATE_NAME FROM M_BACKUP_CATALOG ORDER BY SYS_START_TIME" 
 | SYS_START_TIME | BACKUP_ID | ENTRY_TYPE_NAME | STATE_NAME |
| ----------------------------- | -------------------- | -------------------- | ---------- |
| 2026-11-14 09:10:40.028000000 | 1794647440024 | complete data backup | successful |
| 2026-11-14 09:23:48.304000000 | 1794648228304 | log backup | successful |
| 2026-11-14 09:23:48.329000000 | 1794648228329 | log backup | successful | 
 And the tenant's active root keys are PRD's, same hashes as the file: 
 hdbnsutil -printHashedRootKeys --dbid=3 
 Active Key(s) for DBID: 3
PERSISTENCE Root Key: d2c80e38fcd7e5ef3a2c04bdadbb1ad1f5918917f9d04aa8d77f431ed2521849
DPAPI Root Key: 07238d4a9bb865ee513945baa354d5c0064e34d8c16e19befac68886ac3b8809
LOG Root Key: b21c77bd2416035e8372fd1885b2a06846feec43ed5fb2bfe1ac73fbdcde2bcf
BACKUP Root Key: 329926ac1a6f647bbbfaad8c251e28baea1f495e2f83847fb4946bb679de1d4a
done. 
 Second run with test data 
 I created a table on PRD after the first backup, so it can only reach QAS through a new backup. 
 hdbsql -i 00 -d PRD -u SYSTEM -p '<password>' "CREATE COLUMN TABLE RESTORE_TEST (ID INT PRIMARY KEY, NOTE NVARCHAR(100), CREATED_AT TIMESTAMP)"
hdbsql -i 00 -d PRD -u SYSTEM -p '<password>' "INSERT INTO RESTORE_TEST VALUES (1, 'Written on PRD', CURRENT_TIMESTAMP)"

hdbsql -i 00 -d SYSTEMDB -u SYSTEM -p '<password>' \
 "BACKUP DATA FOR PRD USING FILE ('/hana/backup/PRD_test')" 
 For this copy prdadm got its own key, trusted by qasadm, so files go straight into QAS's /hana/backup with the right owner. 
 # On PRD as prdadm
ssh-keygen -t ed25519 -N '' -f ~/.ssh/id_ed25519
cat ~/.ssh/id_ed25519.pub

# On QAS as qasadm - paste the public key line
mkdir -p ~/.ssh && chmod 700 ~/.ssh
echo '<prdadm public key>' >> ~/.ssh/authorized_keys
chmod 600 ~/.ssh/authorized_keys

# On PRD as prdadm
scp /hana/backup/PRD_test_databackup_* qasadm@<qas-private-ip>:/hana/backup/ 
 No root key import this time. The QAS tenant still has PRD's keys from the first recovery. 
 hdbsql -i 00 -d SYSTEMDB -u SYSTEM -p '<password>' "ALTER SYSTEM STOP DATABASE QAS"
hdbsql -i 00 -d SYSTEMDB -u SYSTEM -p '<password>' \
 "RECOVER DATA FOR QAS USING FILE ('/hana/backup/PRD_test') CLEAR LOG"

hdbsql -i 00 -d QAS -u SYSTEM -p '<password>' -A -j "SELECT * FROM RESTORE_TEST" 
 | ID | NOTE | CREATED_AT |
| ----------- | -------------- | ----------------------------- |
| 1 | Written on PRD | 2026-11-14 09:29:25.695000000 |
1 row selected (overall time 7660 usec; server time 432 usec)

items.title: SAP EWM - Vendor-Specific Preferred UoM for Same Material
items.author: Vedant_Gunde
items.text:
Business Case: 
 In many warehouses, the same material is supplied by different vendors in different packaging. For example, Vendor A delivers in drums, while Vendor B delivers it in canisters. The warehouse prefers to handle the material in the unit of measure matching each vendor’s packaging. 
 In SAP EWM, only one Preferred Unit of Measure (PUoM) can be maintained per product in the product master. This makes it difficult to process inbound deliveries from vendors who use different packaging for the same product. 
 This can be solved with BAdI /SCWM/EX_MD_PUOM_DET which lets you determine the Preferred Unit of Measure dynamically based on the vendor (ship-from party), so each EWM delivery is handled in the UoM that matches the vendor’s packaging. 
 Configuration: 
 SCM EWM > EWM > Cross-Process Settings > Warehouse Task > Define Quantity Classifications 
 SCM EWM > EWM > Master Data > Product > Define Unit of Measure Attributes 
 Master Data: 
 Material Master/ Product master created with BUOM as Liter and AUOM as per below. (MM01 and /SCWM/MAT1). 

 No Preferred UoM maintained in product master. 
 Development: 
 Implemented BADI /SCWM/EX_MD_PUOM_DET with method Determine_PUoM. 

 Sample Code: METHOD /scwm/if_ex_md_puom_det~determine_puom.

 DATA: lv_vendor TYPE lifnr,
 lv_new_uom TYPE meinh,
 lv_base_uom TYPE meinh,
 lv_base_qty TYPE menge_d,
 lv_new_qty TYPE menge_d,
 lv_matnr TYPE matnr,
 lv_umrez TYPE marm-umrez, " numerator
 lv_umren TYPE marm-umren. " denominator

 CHECK iv_lgnum = 'V001'. " <-- change to your new warehouse number if it changed

 " Material number: use the internal (padded) format of your system.
 " Change this value to the actual MATNR of GROUNDNUT OIL (check MARA).
 CONSTANTS: lc_matnr TYPE matnr VALUE 'GROUNDNUT OIL'.

 CHECK is_dlv_item-productno = lc_matnr.

 lv_matnr = is_dlv_item-productno.

 " Determine preferred UoM based on vendor (ship-from)
 lv_vendor = iv_ship_from.
 " Vendor numbers are stored with leading zeros (LIFNR = 10 chars)
 lv_vendor = |{ lv_vendor ALPHA = IN }|.

 CASE lv_vendor.
 WHEN '0253400010'.
 lv_new_uom = 'DR'. " Drum
 WHEN '0253400011'.
 lv_new_uom = 'KAN'. " Canister
 WHEN OTHERS.
 RETURN.
 ENDCASE.

 " Nothing to do if delivery is already in the preferred UoM
 CHECK cv_uom <> lv_new_uom.

 lv_base_uom = 'L'.

 " Step 1: Convert current UoM -> base UoM (L)
 IF cv_uom = lv_base_uom.
 lv_base_qty = cv_qty.
 ELSE.
 CALL FUNCTION 'MD_CONVERT_MATERIAL_UNIT'
 EXPORTING
 i_matnr = lv_matnr
 i_in_me = cv_uom
 i_out_me = lv_base_uom
 i_menge = cv_qty
 IMPORTING
 e_menge = lv_base_qty
 EXCEPTIONS
 error_in_application_log = 1
 error = 2
 OTHERS = 3.
 IF sy-subrc <> 0.
 RETURN.
 ENDIF.
 ENDIF.

 " Step 2: Convert base UoM (L) -> preferred UoM via direct MARM read
 SELECT SINGLE umrez umren
 FROM marm
 INTO (lv_umrez, lv_umren)
 WHERE matnr = lv_matnr
 AND meinh = lv_new_uom.

 IF sy-subrc <> 0 OR lv_umrez IS INITIAL.
 " Conversion not maintained in MM02 -> Additional Data -> Units of Measure
 RETURN.
 ENDIF.

 " MARM logic: 1 alt. UoM = UMREZ / UMREN base UoM
 " Example: DR -> UMREZ = 15, UMREN = 1 => 1 DR = 15 L
 " 30 L * 1 / 15 = 2 DR
 lv_new_qty = lv_base_qty * lv_umren / lv_umrez.

 " Update the changing parameters
 cv_uom = lv_new_uom.
 cv_qty = lv_new_qty.

ENDMETHOD. 
 Note: This is just a sample code which can be modified and improved as per requirement. I'm functional Consultant, I took help from AI to write and optimize code as per my prompt. 😉 
 The example here uses hardcoded vendor numbers to keep the logic easy to follow. For production use, consider moving the vendor-to-UoM mapping into a custom table so that business users or administrators can maintain it, and extend the logic to more products and warehouses. 
 Testing: 
 1) Create 2 PO from 2 different Vendors (ME21N) 

 2) Create Inbound delivery in ERP (VL31N) 

 3) Inbound delivery Replicated to EWM (/SCWM/MON OR /SCWM/PRDI) 

 4) Receive HU received from Vendor (/SCWM/RFUI) 

 Available stock in Monitor (/SCWM/MON) 

 Conclusion: 
 With a single Preferred UoM per product in the EWM product master, that used to mean manual corrections or workarounds. With BAdI /SCWM/EX_MD_PUOM_DET the decision moves into the delivery process itself. The delivery is created in the base UoM, and EWM converts it to the vendor’s packaging automatically. No product master changes, no manual rework, and no confusion on the warehouse floor.

items.author: xuqi_fangaf39f1
items.text:
Hi sap, 
 During the go-live transition, whilst 3F0 SCOPE is enabled, how can opening work-in-progress be imported whilst ensuring consistency with the amounts in the ‘Work-in-progress’ financial account in the legacy system (for each production order)? 
 上线切换在启用 3F0 SCOPE 的情况下，如何导入期初在制品，同时能保证与原系统财务发在制品科目金额（每张生产订单）保持一致.

items.author: xuqi_fangaf39f1
items.text:
Hi sap, 
 When switching to the live system with 5MQ SCOPE enabled, how can opening stock for goods dispatched or in transit be imported whilst ensuring consistency with the amounts recorded under the ‘goods dispatched’ account in the original system’s financial records (for each sales order)? 
 上线切换在启用 5MQ SCOPE 的情况下，如何导入期初发出商品或在途库存，同时能保证与原系统财务发出商品科目金额（每张销售订单）保持一致.

items.title: Why OData/RAP Service Changes Often Require Metadata Cache Clean, Avoid Cache Problems in Production
items.author: anupkumarbharti
items.text: Introduction : One of the most common frustrations for SAP developers is this scenario: I changed my CDS view, RAP BO, service definition, or service binding. The activation was successful, but the UI or consumer system still behaves as if nothing changed The root cause is usually metadata caching.

items.author: JasonLu
items.text: I ran 500 invoice pairs through SAP RPT-1.6 and Cohere Command A Reasoning Model to see which handles duplicate detection better. The results were more nuanced than I expected, and one failure revealed something important about how tabular AI actually works.

items.author: xuqi_fangaf39f1
items.text:
Hi sap, 
 Enquiry regarding the method for importing opening provisional estimates (GR/IR) account details during the go-live transition. 
 Ensure that the provisional (GR/IR) accounts match the detailed amounts in the original system’s accounts (linked to each purchase order), whilst enabling subsequent invoice verification or the settlement of provisional accounts to proceed smoothly. 
 上线切换期初暂估（GR/IR)科目明细导入方法咨询

items.title: 5 things I learned facilitating SAP's Agentic AI training in 2026
items.author: Sudha_Surendran
items.text:
5 things I learned facilitating SAP's Agentic AI training across Ireland in 2026 
 In July 2026 I made a decision to actively rebuild my SAP AI skills. Four months later I had facilitated five two-day Agentic AI sessions, earned my C_JSD (Joule Studio Developer) certification, and stood in front of hundreds of SAP professionals teaching them how to build Joule agents. This post is not about what I taught them. It is about the five things they taught me. 
 Point 1 : Every room had a moment where the AI stopped being theoretical 
 In every session, there was a point where a participant stopped typing and said something like "wait, this actually works." It was never the demo that did it. It was the moment they built something themselves, even something small, and it responded intelligently. The energy in the room shifted. What had been theoretical for weeks became something they could see, touch, and imagine using. The excitement on people's faces in that moment is something I will not forget. Not because it was impressive technology, but because you could see them thinking about their own work, their own problems, their own teams. 
 The training gives people permission to start. It gives them the hands-on time to try, to fail safely, to get their questions answered in real time. And in that moment when something works for the first time, something shifts. They stop waiting for someone else to figure this out. They become the person who is going to figure it out. I know this because the same thing happened to me. 
 The insight: The gap between knowing AI exists and believing it can solve your business problem closes in a hands-on session, not in a presentation. The sooner we can create that moment for people, the better. 
 Point 2 : The question that stopped every room: Who owns the agent's output? 
 Every single session someone asked a version of this question. It came up in different forms: "If the agent makes a mistake, who is responsible?" "Can we trust this in a production workflow?" "What happens when the agent does something unexpected?" The room went quiet. I could see people nodding. This was the real question underneath all the excitement about agentic AI. 
 My answer surprised a few people: the agent does not own anything. It never did. The same person who would have walked into the CEO's office if a badly configured workflow caused that mistake will still walk in. What changes with agentic AI is not where responsibility sits. It is where in the process you need to be paying attention. 
 In Joule Studio, this translates into two things you define when you build an agent: guardrails and human-in-the-loop checkpoints. Guardrails define the boundaries: what data the agent can access, what actions it can take on its own, what it must stop and ask a human before doing. Human-in-the-loop checkpoints are the moments you deliberately build into the workflow where a person reviews, approves, and owns the decision before the agent executes. 
 Think about a regulated workflow, the kind where every action needs a formal sign-off. The agent does the research, prepares the documentation, checks it against the relevant standards. The human reads it, approves it, and their name goes on it. The audit trail records the person, not the agent. 
 When I explained it this way, the follow-up question changed. It stopped being "who is responsible?" and became "where do I put my checkpoint?" That is the shift from fear to design thinking. And once a room makes that shift, you can actually start building something. 
 The insight: The biggest barrier to agentic AI adoption in enterprise is not technology. It is accountability and trust. Organizations need governance frameworks before they need agents. 
 Point 3 : Token efficiency is the new performance tuning, and SAP developers already know how to think about it 
 Performance tuning was a critical discipline in any SAP implementation. I remember spending hours running traces, analysing execution plans, hunting down the one SELECT statement that was dragging an entire report to its knees. Every unnecessary field in a query, every missing index, every unbounded loop. It all had a cost, and experienced developers felt that cost instinctively. They designed with resource efficiency in mind without even thinking about it. 
 That instinct maps directly to one of the most important concepts in agentic AI development: token efficiency. Every prompt you write, every agent instruction you define, every skill you compose : these consume tokens. And tokens cost time, money, and performance. Writing prompts and agent instructions that are lean and purposeful is not just good practice, it is the difference between an agent that scales and one that breaks under load. 
 In the sessions we introduced the CRISP framework as a structured way to think about prompting, making sure every prompt has clear Context, a defined Role, precise Instructions, the right Specifics, and a stated Purpose. We also spent time on context engineering: understanding what information you actually need to pass to the agent at each step, and what you can leave out. Just like you would not SELECT * when you only need three fields, you do not flood an agent with context it does not need to complete its task. 
 What struck me every time was how quickly experienced SAP developers picked this up. They have been thinking about resource efficiency for decades. An ABAP developer who spent years optimising SELECT statements already has the mental model : they just need to point it at a different problem. The mindset is the same: be precise, be intentional, and never ask the system for more than you need. SAP's existing talent base is far more ready for this than they think. 
 The insight: Token efficiency is not just a cost concern; it is a design discipline. And SAP's developer community already has the muscle memory for it. 
 Point 4 : MCP tools changed how I think about integration and how I explain it to customers 
 Model Context Protocol is one of the hardest concepts to land in the sessions. When I first encountered it I sat with it for days. I read it, re-read it, tried to explain it to myself, and still felt like something was slightly out of focus. It was only when I had to stand in front of a room and teach it, five times to five different audiences, that the right way to explain it finally emerged. 
 The analogy that worked: "An MCP tool is like a well-defined API contract, but instead of a developer calling it, an AI agent decides when to call it and what to pass." 
 That single sentence unlocked it for most people. But what made it land differently in each room was knowing the audience before I walked in. Before any session started, I made a point of understanding the background of the people in the room. If the group was from an integration-heavy background, I connected MCP to API Management and event-driven architecture, patterns they already knew and trusted. If they were from an application development background, I leaned on the contract analogy. The concept was the same. The entry point changed. 
 What I came to realise through this process is that MCP is not a new idea. It is integration thinking with an AI decision layer on top. The principles SAP practitioners already understand, well-defined interfaces, clear input and output contracts, separation of concerns, all apply. The one thing that is genuinely new is who initiates the call. It used to be a developer. Now it is an agent. That is a significant shift in how you design, but it is not a shift that requires you to throw away twenty years of integration knowledge. You build on it. 
 The insight: You do not need to unlearn integration knowledge to understand MCPs. You need to reframe it: the caller is now an AI agent, not a human developer. 
 Point 5 : Teaching something is the fastest way to learn it, especially when 25 people are asking questions you have not thought of 
 I want to be honest about something. When I started facilitating in August, I was still consolidating my own understanding. I had attended sessions, I had prepared, but there were corners of this material I had not fully explored. I knew that going in. 
 What I did not expect was how thoroughly the participants would explore those corners for me. 
 After every session my mind was buzzing. Not from the content I delivered, but from the questions they asked. Questions I had not anticipated, angles I had not considered, connections to their specific domains that I had never thought to make. I would come home, open my laptop, and sit with those questions until I had proper answers. Before each new session I went back through the material with fresh eyes, looking for what I might have missed, preparing for the version of the question I had not heard yet. By the third session, the preparation itself had become a form of learning. By the fifth, I was not just delivering content anymore. The discussions in the room were shaping it. 
 In some ways I learned more from those five sessions than I did from all the material I studied before them. The participants brought their real problems, their real scepticism, and their real curiosity. That is not something you can prepare for. It is something you learn to welcome. 
 The insight: If you want to accelerate your learning in any technology, find a way to teach it. The learners will do the rest. 
 I started 2026 as an AI learner. By the middle of the year I had shifted focus entirely to agentic AI. I am ending it as a practitioner, a trainer, and someone with more questions than when I started, which I have learned to take as a good sign. There are more sessions ahead and more to learn. 
 If you are building or exploring agentic AI with SAP and want to compare notes, reach out. The conversation is always more interesting than the slides.

deep_dives.title: Diagnosing stale metadata after activating a RAP service change
deep_dives.explanation:
The post (ref 5) describes the symptom: activation succeeds, but the consumer behaves as if nothing changed. It names a metadata cache as the cause without saying which one. The text gives no transaction, report or API, so the specifics below are a diagnostic approach, not facts from the post.

Start by asking what changed on the server. Activating a CDS view, service definition or behavior definition changes repository objects. A service binding exposes the service, and consumers read its `$metadata` document. Candidate holders of old metadata are the server-side Gateway metadata cache, the browser, the Fiori launchpad, and any consumer-side proxy or generated client. The post does not say which one applies.

A workable method is to fetch `$metadata` directly, for example in a fresh browser session or a REST client, and compare it with what the UI sees. If the direct response is current and the UI is stale, the problem is on the client side. If the direct response is stale, look at the server. Repeat the check after each cache-clean step to see which step fixed it. Take the actual cache-clean procedure from SAP documentation for your release, since the post does not provide it.
key_concepts: Candidate cache layers: Gateway, browser, launchpad, consumer proxy

post_drafts.title: Activated, but UI still shows old behaviour?
post_drafts.text:
*Activated your RAP/CDS change but the Fiori UI looks unchanged?*

A community post blames metadata caching. It names no cache and gives no steps, so treat it as a hint, not a diagnosis.

Quick way to find the stale layer:
1. Open the service's `$metadata` URL in a fresh session
2. Compare it with what the app sees
3. Current in the direct call = client-side cache
4. Stale in the direct call = look server-side

*Prove it, don't assume it.*

https://community.sap.com/t5/technology-blog-posts-by-members/why-odata-rap-service-changes-often-require-metadata-cache-clean-avoid/ba-p/14522540

interview_questions.question: After you activate a change to a CDS view and RAP BO, the Fiori app still shows old behaviour. How do you find out where the stale state is?
interview_questions.answer: Separate server state from client state. First confirm the objects are active and the service binding is published. Then request `$metadata` for the service directly, in a fresh session or a REST client, and compare it with what the app uses. If the direct response shows the change, the staleness is on the client side, such as browser, launchpad or a consumer proxy. If it does not, the server side needs investigation, including any Gateway metadata cache. Clear one layer at a time and recheck `$metadata` after each step, so you know which step fixed it. Take the exact cache-clean procedure from SAP documentation for your release instead of guessing. Note that the source post only asserts caching as the cause and does not prove it.

interview_questions.question: Which artefacts are involved when you expose a RAP BO as an OData service, and which of them can affect what a consumer sees in `$metadata`?
interview_questions.answer: The CDS data model and projection views define the entities and fields. The behavior definition and projection define the operations and actions. The service definition selects which entities are exposed. The service binding publishes the service for a protocol such as OData V2 or V4 UI. A change to any of these can change `$metadata`. Activation updates the repository, but a consumer sees the change only if it reads fresh metadata. That is why you check the raw `$metadata` response after changes. The source post lists these same artefacts as the ones whose changes appear not to take effect.

interview_questions.question: A colleague says 'it's just metadata cache, clear it in production after each transport.' How do you respond as a technical lead?
interview_questions.answer: I would ask for evidence first. A blanket cache clean after each transport treats a symptom without a confirmed cause, and the source post does not say which cache is meant or how to clear it. I would reproduce the problem, compare `$metadata` from the server with what the client holds, and identify the layer. If a server cache is confirmed, I would document the SAP-supported procedure for our release and add it to the transport or go-live checklist. I would also check whether the transport is complete, for example that the service binding and all dependent objects arrived. A clear, verified runbook is better than a habit based on an assumption.
